answer.sourceLine: A genuine fragment of Heraclitus (Diels–Kranz 22 B40), preserved as a direct quotation in Diogenes Laertius, “Lives of the Eminent Philosophers” 9.1. This exact English wording is the opening clause of R. D. Hicks’ Loeb Classical Library translation (1925); the fuller sentence goes on to name Hesiod, Pythagoras, Xenophanes and Hecataeus.

source.excerpt: Much learning does not teach understanding; else would it have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras, or, again, Xenophanes and Hecataeus.
trail: The line is catalogued as a genuine fragment — Diels–Kranz 22 B40 — and listed among the authentic sayings on Wikiquote’s Heraclitus page.

Its source is Diogenes Laertius, who quotes it directly in his life of Heraclitus; the LacusCurtius text reads “Much learning does not teach understanding; else would it have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras…”
That exact English is R. D. Hicks’ 1925 Loeb rendering, reproduced on Wikisource; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy treats B40 as authentic.
source.excerptNote: The one-liner that circulates online is only the first clause. Heraclitus’ point lands in the second half: he names four famously erudite men — the poet Hesiod and the thinkers Pythagoras, Xenophanes and Hecataeus — as proof that piling up information is no guarantee of insight.
source.rightsNote: The displayed English is R. D. Hicks’ translation for the Loeb Classical Library, first published in 1925. A translation carries its own copyright, but a 1925 work is in the public domain in the United States (anything published before 1931). The underlying Greek of Heraclitus is, of course, long out of copyright.

author.name: Heraclitus
author.heading: Heraclitus of Ephesus
author.metaLine: c. 540 – c. 480 BC · Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher of Ephesus
author.bio: Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic philosopher from Ephesus in Ionia, nicknamed in antiquity ho Skoteinos (“the Obscure”) for his riddling style. He is remembered for the doctrine of universal flux — the idea that all things are in constant change — and for his emphasis on the logos and the unity of opposites. His single book, conventionally titled On Nature, survives only in fragments quoted by later writers such as Diogenes Laertius, which is how this saying reaches us.

misattribution.heading: Quote vs. misquote
misattribution.intro: The author here is not in doubt — this really is Heraclitus. The wrinkles are about wording: the popular one-liner is a truncation, and different translators phrase the fragment differently.

items.why: Brainyquote, Goodreads and similar sites print only “Much learning does not teach understanding,” dropping the clause that gives it force — “else would it have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras, or, again, Xenophanes and Hecataeus” (Diogenes Laertius 9.1, Hicks).

The exact English depends on who is translating. Hicks’ Loeb has “Much learning does not teach understanding,” while the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy renders B40 as “Learning many things does not teach understanding.” The idea — a rebuke of mere polymathy — is the same.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the saying is authentically Heraclitus (fragment B40, quoted by Diogenes Laertius 9.1); this specific English is R. D. Hicks’ 1925 Loeb wording, usually shown shorn of its second half.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Heraclitus aimed this barb at a culture that prized the accumulation of facts and travelers’ lore. By naming Hesiod, Pythagoras, Xenophanes and Hecataeus — a poet, a mathematician-mystic, a philosopher-poet and an early geographer-historian, all celebrated for the breadth of what they knew — he argued that erudition without insight is hollow.
The line has had a long afterlife as a caution against confusing information with comprehension, quoted everywhere from philosophy classrooms to modern debates about data and wisdom.
context.detailsSummary: About the four men he names
detailsBody: Hesiod — archaic Greek poet (Theogony, Works and Days). Pythagoras — philosopher and mathematician. Xenophanes — philosopher-poet who criticized anthropomorphic gods. Hecataeus of Miletus — early historian and geographer. All four were bywords for learning, which is precisely why Heraclitus picks them.
